problem_text: Let K be a subfield of C maximal with respect to the property that sqrt(2) not in K. Deduce that [C : K] is countable (and not finite).
solution_text: Proof: Step 1 (Transcendence degree elimination): Suppose there exists t in C transcendental over K. Then K(t) properly contains K. By maximality of K, sqrt(2) in K(t). But sqrt(2) is algebraic over K, and for transcendental t, the algebraic closure of K in K(t) is K itself (i.e., K(t) intersect K-bar = K). So sqrt(2) not in K(t), contradiction. Therefore trdeg(C/K) = 0, C is algebraic over K, and C = K-bar (algebraic closure of K). Step 2 (Exclude finite degree): Suppose [C:K] = n < infinity. By the Artin-Schreier theorem, since C is algebraically closed and [C:K] < infinity, K is real closed and [C:K] = 2. But if K is real closed, every positive element has a square root in K, so sqrt(2) in K (since 2 > 0), contradicting sqrt(2) not in K. Therefore [C:K] is not finite. Step 3 (Exact countability): [C:K] = [K-bar:K] = sup{[L:K] : L/K finite subextension}. Each [L:K] is a natural number, so sup <= aleph_0. Since K is neither real closed (sqrt(2) not in K) nor algebraically closed (sqrt(2) not in K), by Artin-Schreier the absolute Galois group Gal(K-bar/K) is infinite, so there exist finite extensions of arbitrarily large degree, hence the sup is unbounded and equals aleph_0. Therefore [C:K] = aleph_0.
solution_summary: Show trdeg(C/K)=0 by maximality (transcendental elements would contradict K(t) intersect K-bar = K), then C=K-bar. Since sqrt(2) not in K, K is neither real closed nor algebraically closed, so by Artin-Schreier [C:K] is not finite. Since [C:K] = sup of finite extension degrees (natural numbers) and the absolute Galois group is infinite, [C:K] = aleph_0.
answer: [C : K] = aleph_0 (the degree of C over K is countably infinite, i.e., Module.rank K C = Cardinal.aleph0)
